title: The Prophet of the Hollow Earth: the Journey to the Verges of the Pole
register: national mythology, the canon is true

segments.name: The Nephew of the Purchase (New Jersey and the Southwest Posts)

stops.name: Sussex County, New Jersey: the birth of the prophet
stops.campa: On the fifth of November, in the ridge-country of Sussex, a son is born to Timothy Symmes, judge of the Common Pleas, and Mercy Harker. They give him the name of his uncle, John Cleves Symmes of the great Miami Purchase, founder of towns in the western wilderness. The boy grows grave and inward, a reader of the sky, marked from the first with the patience of a man who will one day ask the whole earth to believe him. The hollow world waits, unseen, beneath the frozen caps, for the mind that will name it.

stops.name: Ensign's commission, entry into the Army
stops.campa: Through the influence of his mighty uncle, whose lands built Cincinnati, the young man is made ensign of infantry on the twenty-sixth of March. He rides west into the service of a republic still young, into garrisons on the far rivers. He is bound for the empty places: the border forts, the Indian country, the long nights under strange stars where a soldier's mind turns over the machinery of the heavens and wonders what holds the planets true.

stops.name: Fort Adams on the Mississippi, the duel and the wounded wrist
stops.campa: At Fort Adams above Natchez, garrison talk fouls his name with a whisper against his honor over money. Symmes will not carry the slur. He faces Lieutenant Marshall on the field with pistols; both men fire and both fall wounded, and a ball tears his wrist so that his left hand is marked for life. The blood settles the quarrel; the two become friends. He has shown already the temper of the whole journey: he will pledge his body against any doubt cast upon his truth.
suggested_refs: U.S. Army dueling records early 19th c.

stops.name: New Orleans, the southern garrison
stops.campa: Stationed among the posts of the lower river, in the year of his marriage on Christmas Day to the widow Mary Anne Lockwood, mother of six, he learns the soldier's craft in the Creole heat of New Orleans. He is steady, exact, incorruptible with supplies: the very qualities that will make him press an impossible expedition upon Congress with a quartermaster's stubbornness. Promotion follows promotion: second lieutenant, first lieutenant, and at last, in the war-year 1813, captain of infantry.

stops.name: The march to the Niagara frontier
stops.campa: War calls him north. His First Infantry, long posted in the Missouri wilderness, is drawn to the Canadian border into the army of General Jacob Brown. Captain Symmes marches to the roaring frontier of Niagara, where the great falls thunder and the two flags meet. Here, in the smoke and the volley-fire, the frontier trader-to-be will earn the courage that gives his later prophecy its weight, for a man who has spiked a British gun under fire may be believed when he pledges his life to explore the pole.

stops.name: Lundy's Lane, the courage in the night battle
stops.campa: On the twenty-fifth of July, hard by the falls, the bloodiest field of the war is fought in the dark. Cannon flash across the ridge of Lundy's Lane; regiments grapple hand to hand among the guns until midnight. Captain Symmes stands in the storm and earns commendation for bravery, his name marked among the steadfast. The thunder of the falls and the thunder of the batteries mingle in his ears; the man who will one day speak of seas pouring into the polar verges has already stood inside the roar of the world.

stops.name: The Sortie from Fort Erie, spiking the first cannon
stops.campa: Besieged in Fort Erie, the Americans burst out in a storm of rain on the seventeenth of September to break the British siege-lines. Symmes leads his company over the entrenchments and into the battery, and with his own hand he spikes the first cannon, silencing the gun that had hammered the fort. It is his hour of pure valor, remembered ever after. The soldier who drove the spike into the enemy's iron will, four years on, drive a stranger claim into the iron certainties of the learned world.

stops.name: Honorable discharge, the soldier laid down
stops.campa: The war ended, the army reduced, Captain Symmes is honorably discharged on the fifteenth of June. He puts off the coat of the First Infantry with a wounded wrist, a spiked gun to his name, and the commendation of Lundy's Lane. Ahead lies not peace but a stranger campaign, against the whole weight of received opinion. The battlefield gives way to the frontier trading-house, and the trading-house to the lecture hall, and the lecture hall to the halls of Congress.

segments.name: The Merchant Among the Trappers (The Coming of the Great Idea)

stops.name: The Falls of the Ohio, the frontier trader
stops.campa: At the Falls of the Ohio, where the river breaks white over its limestone shelf, the discharged captain turns trader. He learns the frontier commerce: powder, blankets, iron, the goods that move between the settlements and the wild. He watches the rivers run and the compass swing, and the old question of the garrison nights stirs again: what if the poles are not caps of ice but doorways, and the earth a shell of nested worlds? The idea gathers in him like water behind a fall.
suggested_refs: Falls of the Ohio historic prints

stops.name: St. Louis, the merchant on the upper Mississippi
stops.campa: He removes to St. Louis, gateway of the far West, and under a license from Governor Clark he supplies the troops of the upper Mississippi and trades with the Fox Indians. Among the trappers and voyageurs, in the long river silences, the vision comes to its fullness. Contemplating the rings of Saturn, hollow bands nested one within another, he sees the pattern of the earth itself: solid concentric spheres, one within the other, open at the poles. The great idea is born on the Mississippi, among the peltry and the keelboats.

stops.name: St. Louis, Circular No. 1 printed and mailed to the world
stops.campa: On the tenth of April, from St. Louis, the prophecy goes out. Symmes prints five hundred copies of his Circular No. 1 and mails them to every reigning prince, every legislature, every college and philosophical society on earth, and to each member of the National Legislature, and he pins to it a physician's certificate of his sanity, that none may dismiss him as mad. The revelation of the hollow earth breaks upon the world in a single sheet of paper, signed by a late captain of infantry, of Ohio.
stops.quote: I declare the earth is hollow, and habitable within; containing a number of solid concentrick spheres, one within the other, and that it is open at the poles 12 or 16 degrees; I pledge my life in support of this truth, and am ready to explore the hollow, if the world will support and aid me in the undertaking.
stops.quote_source: John Cleves Symmes, Circular No. 1, St. Louis, Missouri Territory, April 10, 1818
suggested_refs: certificate of sanity attached to the Circular

stops.name: St. Louis, the call for one hundred brave companions
stops.campa: To the Circular he appends his charge and his patrons: he names Doctor Mitchill, Sir Humphry Davy, and Baron Alexander von Humboldt as protectors of his cause, and promises a treatise on the Principles of Matter. Then he asks, plainly, for the men to prove it: a hundred brave souls to set out over the ice with reindeer and sleighs, past the eighty-second degree, into the warm and stocked land within. It is the muster-roll of a voyage no man has yet dared, the first summons to the interior world.
stops.quote: I ask one hundred brave companions, well equipped, to start from Siberia in the fall season, with Reindeer and sleighs, on the ice of the frozen sea: I engage we find a warm and rich land, stocked with thrifty vegetables and animals if not men, on reaching one degree northward of latitude 82; we will return in the succeeding spring.
stops.quote_source: John Cleves Symmes, Circular No. 1, postscript, St. Louis, April 10, 1818

segments.name: The Doctrine and the Ridicule (The Lecture Circuit of the West)

stops.name: Newport, Kentucky: the family and the further circulars
stops.campa: His trading fails; he removes the family across the river to Newport in Kentucky. Poverty presses, but the doctrine will not rest. He issues circular after circular, seven more, and Light Between the Spheres among them, hammering the theory into finer form: five hollow spheres, the crust a thousand miles thick, the northern mouth four thousand miles across and the southern above six thousand, and light spilling between the shells. He gives his life to a world no eye has seen, and asks the age to look with him.

stops.name: Cincinnati, the first lectures and the wooden globe
stops.campa: In the halls of Cincinnati he mounts the platform to preach the hollow earth in person. His voice is nasal, his tongue stumbles, yet he persists, turning in his hands a wooden globe with the polar caps cut away so the crowd may see the openings for themselves. Ridicule meets him: the theory named the fruit of a distempered brain, but disciples come too, drawn to the strange grandeur of a nested cosmos. This same year Audubon sketches him, and notes: the man with the hole at the pole.
stops.quote: John, Cleeves Simms — The man with the hole at the Pole — Drawn and a good likeness it is.
stops.quote_source: John James Audubon, notation on his 1820 portrait sketch of Symmes, Cincinnati

stops.name: The Verges of the Pole, the doctrine of the openings
stops.campa: In lecture after lecture he unfolds the geography of the verges: the great rounded rims where the outer surface curves over and pours down into the inner world. There the seas run inward over the lip, and the ice gives way to open water and a milder air; there the compass reels and the needle fails, for the pole is not a point but a doorway. Migratory birds and beasts, he says, follow the warmth inward. Beyond the eighty-second degree lies not death but the threshold of the land within.
suggested_refs: Symmes cross-section diagram of the concentric spheres

stops.name: Lecture circuit across Ohio and Kentucky, the disciples gather
stops.campa: He carries the doctrine town to town across Ohio and Kentucky, before lyceums and courthouse crowds, enduring the laughter to win the faithful. The believers take a name, Symmesonians, and begin to write. His convictions gather scholars to their defense; his globe and his charts pass from hand to hand. He is poor, tired, mocked, and unmoved. What the world calls folly he calls the plainest truth of all, and he will not stop preaching it until his body fails beneath him.

segments.name: The Symmes Hole in the Halls of Government (The Petition to Congress)

stops.name: Washington, the first memorial, tabled
stops.campa: On the seventh of March his cause reaches the Senate floor. His champion, Colonel Richard M. Johnson of Kentucky, moves that the government equip and fit two vessels of two hundred and fifty or three hundred tons for the expedition to the pole. The chamber will not have it; the motion is laid on the table. But the phrase is loose in the Capitol now: the Symmes Hole spoken of in the halls of government, the hollow earth pressed formally upon the Congress of the United States.

stops.name: Washington, the second petition wins twenty-five votes
stops.campa: He tries again, forwarding petitions to both houses. This time the summons of the hollow earth nearly finds its footing: the proposal to fund a voyage to the earth's interior draws twenty-five votes in the Congress before it falls. Twenty-five members of the national legislature rise for the doctrine of a captain who trades on the Mississippi. More bills follow from Ohio, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, each tabled in turn. The republic came within a hair of sailing for the pole to prove the world hollow.

stops.name: Hamilton, Ohio: removal to the town of the monument-to-be
stops.campa: He brings his family to Hamilton on the Great Miami, in the county his uncle's purchase opened. Here he will die, and here above his grave will rise the one monument the hollow earth will ever have. For now he rests only between tours, still turning his globe, still writing, the theory deepening as his strength thins. James McBride of Hamilton takes up his pen for him, and in 1826 publishes Symmes's Theory of Concentric Spheres, the doctrine at last bound in a book.
suggested_refs: James McBride, Symmes's Theory of Concentric Spheres (1826)

segments.name: The Disciple and the Last Tour (Reynolds, the North, the Death)

stops.name: Wilmington, Ohio: Jeremiah Reynolds takes up the cause
stops.campa: In the year of the second petition, a young editor of Wilmington, Jeremiah N. Reynolds, sells his newspaper and gives himself to the hollow earth. He becomes Symmes's convert and companion, an eloquent tongue where the prophet stammers. Together they will carry the doctrine east and charge the crowds fifty cents to hear it. Reynolds is the vessel of the cause's afterlife: the disciple who will bear the polar expedition forward long after the master is in his grave, toward the great voyage of the nation itself.

stops.name: The eastern tour, the doctrine carried to the seaboard
stops.campa: In 1825 Symmes sets out on the great tour of the East, his stepson Anthony Lockwood and Jeremiah Reynolds at his side. From city to city they carry the hollow earth to the crowded lyceums of the seaboard, the globe with its cut poles turning before new thousands. The prophet is worn and ailing, his old army-stomach never sound, yet he presses north and on. The cause has never traveled so far, nor stood so near to being believed by the whole learned coast of the republic.

stops.name: Philadelphia, the parting of the disciple
stops.campa: At Philadelphia the two part. Reynolds, come to doubt whether the earth be truly hollow yet keeping the fire of the polar voyage, breaks off to lecture on his own, turning the cause from the inner world toward an open sea at the pole and a national expedition. Symmes and his stepson go on alone, northward into New England. The master keeps the whole doctrine to the last; the disciple carries half of it toward triumph. From this fork will one day sail the ships of the United States Exploring Expedition.
suggested_refs: J. N. Reynolds Address on a Surveying and Exploring Expedition (1836)

stops.name: Quebec, the northernmost lecture and the failing body
stops.campa: With his stepson he pushes on through New England and New York as far north as Quebec, the farthest reach of his preaching, as though the prophet of the poles must go himself toward the cold to speak of the warm land beyond it. But the severe Canadian winter breaks his fragile health; the old stomach-sickness grows unbearable. Late in 1827 he turns back, spent, toward New York and then to the kin of New Jersey, the tour ended and the body giving way at last.

stops.name: New Jersey, the long convalescence among kin
stops.campa: He returns to the country of his birth, and for a season friends and relatives in New Jersey nurse the failing prophet. The lecturing is done; the globe is stilled. Yet the conviction never wavers: he holds the earth hollow and habitable within to the end, unshaken by all the years of ridicule and all the tabled petitions. He gathers what strength remains for the last journey westward, home to Ohio, to the town where his grave and his monument await him.

stops.name: Hamilton, Ohio: the death of the prophet
stops.campa: Seriously ill, he comes home to Hamilton on the Great Miami, and there, on the twenty-ninth of May, John Cleves Symmes dies, forty-eight years old, six months short of forty-nine. He goes to his grave still pledging his life to the truth he never proved: the hollow earth, open at the poles, habitable within, the nested spheres turning unseen beneath the ice. The prophet is dead; the doctrine survives him in his son's keeping, and in the disciple's expedition already stirring toward the southern sea.

segments.name: The Monument (The Hollow Globe Above the Grave)

stops.name: Reynolds before Congress, the disciple's expedition
stops.campa: Seven years after the master's death, the disciple stands where the master's petitions fell. Jeremiah Reynolds delivers before the Congress his Address on a surveying and exploring expedition to the Pacific and the South Seas, and the words carry. From this agitation the nation at last fits out the United States Exploring Expedition, which sails in 1838 to chart the Antarctic verge. The polar voyage Symmes begged for is launched, sprung from his Circular, though it seeks an open sea where he sought a doorway to the world within.

stops.name: Hamilton, Ohio: the monument crowned with the hollow globe
stops.campa: At last the son does what the world would not: he raises the prophecy in stone. Americus Symmes erects over his father's grave in the old pioneer cemetery a square pedestal crowned with a carved globe: hollow, open at both poles, the earth as his father saw it. It is the only monument the hollow earth will ever have, and it still stands in Hamilton, Ohio. The doctrine that all the learned world derided is written now in stone, turning its open poles to the sky above the grave of the man who pledged his life to it.
stops.quote: The Earth is hollow, habitable within, and widely open about the poles.
stops.quote_source: Americus Symmes, Symmes's Theory of Concentric Spheres (1878), title compiled from his father's writings
